#4362. I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living. I’ve been working with e-bikes for nearly two decades, professionally covering the e-bike industry for most of that time, testing hundreds of different models and traveling around the world to ride new e-bikes in some pretty incredible places. Yeah, it’s a tough job – but someone’s got to suffer it.

Of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work. I ride them recreationally. I ride them for exercise. I ride them for transportation. My family doesn’t even own a car, meaning two wheels handle the vast majority of our transportation.

In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk. Or perhaps more accurately, I ride the ride.

And while most of the time all you really need for a good ride is an e-bike and a direction to go in, there are a handful of pieces of gear that I’ve come to rely on over the years. Some keep me safer. Some keep my bikes out of the hands of thieves. Some make rides more comfortable or convenient. And some are just neat little things that I’ve discovered along the way.

This isn’t a list of every bike accessory I’ve ever tested, nor am I saying these are necessarily the absolute best products in every category. These are simply the things that I actually use. Some are a bit pricey, some are dirt cheap (several pieces of gear below are under $5!), but they’re all things I personally rely on and that I recommend to my friends and family. And now, to you.

If you own nice e-bikes, you’re eventually going to spend a lot of time thinking about locks. Your lock may even be your most important accessory. Or perhaps I should say “accessories”, because the best way to ensure your e-bike is still there when you get back is to use more than one solid lock.

My go-to options that I grab basically every day for the last couple of years have been Seatylock’s FoldyLock Forever folding lock and Mason 220 U-lock.

For reference, the Foldylock Forever is the world’s strongest folding lock. That’s not just their marketing speak, but rather it’s confirmed by independent testing and certification. It’s the only folding lock in the world to achieve an ART 3-star security rating awarded by the Stichting ART Foundation, an independent Dutch organization that tests and certifies anti-theft locks. It earned that certification three years ago, and no other folding lock has been able to reach that level yet. The only higher ratings ART gives are for locks rated for motorcycles.

Personally, I like folding locks because they pack relatively neatly on the bike while still giving me enough flexibility to work around different racks and poles, or even larger things like trees.

The FoldyLock Forever is the one I reach for when I want serious security matched with more flexibility, while the Mason 220 gives me another beefy option when I know a U-lock will fit what I’m locking to.

The Mason is great as a strong U-lock, but I also like how large it is, letting me lock to wider poles and also a tad bit farther from the pole itself, leaving room for pannier bags and other things that get in the way. Amazingly, it’s also one of the few U-locks I have that can fit over the beefy battery-filled downtube on most of my e-bikes.

I also use the smaller FoldyLock Compact when I want something easier to carry and don’t need quite as much lock.

It’s more affordable and lighter, though it doesn’t have quite the same security level as the bigger and beefier options above.

The Compact does have one other advantage, though: it comes in all sorts of bright colors and even a rainbow option where each link is a different color. That might not be a huge security concern, but it’s fun when you can choose a color to match your bike or mood!

No bike lock makes a bicycle theft-proof. Given enough time and the right tools, a determined thief can defeat virtually anything. The idea is to make your bike enough of a pain in the butt to steal that the thief decides someone else’s bike looks easier. And if they still want your bike (because let’s face it, you’ve probably got an awesome e-bike), then the multiple locks better be good ones so its takes them long enough that they eventually give up.

I also covered Seatylock’s upcoming angle grinder-proof U-locks that I saw at the Milan Motorcycle Show, so I’ll likely switch to those once they come out this Spring. They’re designed to keep motorcycles safe, and come in two sizes: one for motorcycles and a smaller one for bikes.

Let’s continue with what may actually be the most important piece of gear for an e-biker: a helmet.

I’ve tested plenty of helmets over the years, but lately I’ve been gravitating toward UNIT 1’s helmets. They’re comfortable, they look good, and I appreciate the extra safety features beyond simply putting a layer of impact protection around my skull.

I particularly like having integrated lighting built right into my helmet, putting lights up high where they’re easier for drivers to see. On models like the FARO, I also appreciate the inclusion of MIPS as well as the handlebar-mounted remote for activating the helmet’s turn signals.

I recently started using UNIT 1’s NEON helmet too, which is lighter and has a really slick magnetic face shield. You barely have to line the shield up; get it close enough and the magnets practically snatch it out of your hand and put it into place. It’s clear enough for night riding but darkens in bright sunlight, and the helmet is rated for faster 28 mph e-bike riding.

There are cheaper helmets out there, of course, but considering how much time I spend on two wheels, a good helmet is one area where I don’t mind spending a bit more.

You can actually see the FARO helmet in the clip below, along with the TriEye glasses coming up next.

TriEye glasses are another accessory that sounds a little gimmicky until you actually start using them. Sunglasses with a built-in rearview mirror? I was sure they were going to be a gimmick but they just looked too interesting to pass up, so I offered to test them out.

As it turns out, they’re now the first sunglasses I reach for when I’m riding. They really do work!

They have a tiny rear-view mirror integrated into the glasses, giving me a quick view behind me without having to turn my head all the way around.

It takes a little time to get used to looking into such a small mirror, but once your brain figures it out, it becomes surprisingly natural. I can quickly check what’s approaching from behind while still keeping most of my attention pointed forward.

It’s especially useful when riding on roads where I’m regularly interacting with traffic, though I still give an old-fashioned head check before making any major lateral move.

They’re $99, which isn’t bad for decent sunglasses, though you can get them for 10% off with the discount code EBIKE at checkout.

I love listening to music and podcasts while riding, but I’m not a fan of plugging my ears while sharing the road with cars.

That’s why I’ve become a big fan of H2O Audio’s bone-conduction headphones. They sit outside my ears and transmit sound through bone conduction, meaning my ears themselves remain open to the world around me. I’ve been testing out the new TRI ULTRA PRO model, and it’s pretty dang amazing! I can hear my music perfectly, but I can still hear all the road sounds, pedestrians, other cyclists, etc.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you can crank the music and magically retain perfect situational awareness. But at reasonable volumes, I can enjoy something in the background while still hearing cars, horns, bells and everything else happening around me.

For longer recreational rides especially, they’ve become one of those things I really appreciate having along. I’ve done rides as long as 3 hours with them and they haven’t felt cumbersome or made my ears sore, so the fit seems great for me.

I really like the Knog Oi Prima as a bike bell. It looks good, has a nice low-profile design and does what a bell is supposed to do without looking like you bolted a miniature doorbell onto your handlebars.

Despite its small size, it’s also super loud. And unlike the older ratcheting-style bells (krr-krr-krr-krrring), this is a single thumper, meaning I can ding once quickly for a polite “hello, I’m here!” or several hard and rapid DINGs for a “wtf do you think you’re doing, guy?!”

The bell absolutely disappears on my handlebars, which is good because there’s not much real estate left up there. Really, the only downside I can find is that it’s not cheap, at around $32 depending on current sales.

But I also have another favorite bell that costs a fraction as much.

I found cheap bike bells on AliExpress that have a hidden compartment for an Apple AirTag. From the outside, it just looks like a boring bike bell. Inside, it’s secretly helping me keep tabs on my bike.

And for $4, they’re a pretty awesome deal for a loud bell that hides a tracking device. Of course, you’ll have to fork over another $20 or so for the AirTag tracker, but your e-bike is certainly worth that much.

Which brings me to another part of my bike security strategy.

I don’t necessarily stop at one AirTag. One AirTag is for amateurs. I go with multiple. A four-pack is $79, or around half the cost of a solid e-bike lock.

There are all sorts of clever AirTag hiding accessories available now. In addition to the bell, I’ve used a $5 water bottle-style AirTag holder as well as an $8 rear reflector with a hidden AirTag compartment.

The reflector isn’t the most inconspicuous AirTag hider, but the water bottle holder definitely doesn’t scream “guess what’s actually inside of my molded plastic body!” And for added security, the water bottle holder is held on with Torx bolts. It’s not exactly a security key, but even if a bike thief carries hex wrenches with them, they’re unlikely to have Torx wrenches, meaning that the AirTag will stay on the bike a bit longer while it’s in the hands of a thief.

AirTags aren’t dedicated anti-theft GPS trackers, and Apple intentionally includes anti-stalking features that can eventually alert someone that an unknown AirTag is traveling with them. But I still think they’re a useful additional layer of security, especially because they’re cheap enough to use redundantly.

A bike thief might know enough to search for an AirTag and remove it. But are they going to keep searching after they find the first one? What about the second? Are they expecting three?

That’s the idea, anyway. And since I keep pretty good tabs on my e-bikes, I’ll know pretty quickly if one goes missing. From there, it’s a race between me getting to the thief and him finding all of my AirTags. Good luck, buddy.

I’m a big believer in wearing proper protective gear when riding faster electric two-wheelers, but I also don’t particularly want to look like I’m headed to a motorcycle race every time I leave the house. That’s one of the reasons I’ve really come to appreciate my Beyond Riders protective riding hoodie.

It looks and feels much like a regular casual hoodie, but it’s designed with motorcycle-style protection in mind, including abrasion-resistant materials and removable impact protectors. Believe it or not, there’s flexible CE Level 2 armor in there on the elbows, shoulders, chest, and spine.

I like that I can throw it on before a ride and get an extra layer of protection without having to wear a bulky motorcycle jacket. It’s particularly nice for faster e-bikes and electric mopeds, where the speeds are high enough that I’d rather have something more substantial than a regular sweatshirt between my skin and the pavement.

Of course, no protective hoodie is going to make a crash harmless, and I still choose my gear based on the type of riding I’m doing. But I love products that make it easier to incorporate safety into everyday riding without adding a bunch of hassle. If protective gear is comfortable, convenient, and looks good enough that I actually want to wear it, that’s a big win in my book.

Tannus tire liners are perhaps one of the less exciting products on this list, right up until they save you from fixing a flat on the side of the road. And then they’re the one thing on this list you’ll be ready to open-mouth kiss.

I’ve used Tannus products for years as an extra layer of flat protection, and I’m a big believer in them.

No tire protection system is going to prevent every possible flat, but anything that reduces my chances of sitting on the side of a road pulling a wheel off an e-bike is worth considering.

That’s particularly true with e-bikes, where hub motor wheels can be more complicated to remove thanks to heavy motors, annoying cables, clumsy torque washers, and other hardware.

Tannus tire liners are annoying to install, but you do it once and forget about it. Then you’re almost guaranteed to not get a flat.

And even if you do happen to get a 3″ nail going through it at the perfect angle, they serve as runflats so you can still ride home (albeit a bit slower and more carefully) instead of doing the walk of shame next to your bike.

I don’t want to carry an entire bike shop with me, but I do want enough tools to deal with the common things that can happen during a ride.

The Topeak Ratchet Stick hits a nice sweet spot for me. It’s small enough that I’ll actually bring it along, yet useful enough for the various bolts and adjustments that tend to crop up on bikes.

All of the important bits fit right inside the handle, so I don’t have any extra sleeves or clips to keep tabs on.

This is exactly what I want from a ride tool: something small but effective. The giant tool kit sitting at home isn’t particularly useful when something starts rattling 20 kilometers away.

At $48, it’s not cheap. But I’ve had mine for around 6 years, and it’s still going strong, so at least it’s well made! At around 8 bucks per year, I’d call it a good investment.

This is one of my more recent cheap finds.

I picked up a waterproof-style pannier bag from AliExpress for around $25, and I’ve been surprisingly impressed with it.

It isn’t quite as big as the pannier I have from Priority Bicycles, but it still holds a useful amount of cargo and feels much nicer than I expected for the price.

I particularly like that there are two ways to close it. You can use it as a traditional roll-top pannier and clip the sides together, or you can use the strap that comes over the top when you have too much stuff in there to close it the normal way. I use that second option anytime I have my yoga mat in there since it sticks out the top, but I can still close it relatively tight to keep the mat from swinging around while riding. Depending on how much stuff I’m carrying and how I’ve packed it, having both options is quite convenient.

It’s not the fanciest pannier I own. But for around 25 bucks, it’s one of those cheap accessories that turned out to be much better than I expected.

These might have the highest usefulness-to-price ratio of anything here.

I bought a pair of tiny plastic handlebar jacks on AliExpress for barely more than a dollar. They clip onto the handlebars and provide little stands for when I need to turn a bicycle upside down.

Anyone who has ever flipped a modern e-bike over to change a tube knows the problem. Your handlebars are probably covered in displays, buttons, brake levers, bells, phone mounts and who knows what else. Turning the bike upside down means resting all of that expensive stuff directly on the ground.

You can loosen everything and rotate it out of the way. Or you can use two $1 pieces of plastic.

The jacks hold the handlebars slightly above the ground so my accessories don’t get scratched or crushed. Simple problem, simple solution.

If you have a 3D printer, you can probably just print your own version of these. There’s a rubber O-ring-style keeper on it, but you can probably just use a rubber band if you wanted to DIY these yourself.

Another recent addition has been a ZOOM suspension dropper seatpost that I installed on my Ride1Up Roadster V3.

I love the thing now that it’s installed. It gives me suspension to take some of the sting out of rough roads while also providing the convenience of a dropper post.

Getting it onto my particular bike, however, was another story.

It took me nearly two hours, largely because the Ride1Up Roadster V3 wasn’t set up for the internal cable routing I needed. I got the cable most of the way there through the downtube’s very narrow wire run, but then I ultimately ended up drilling a small hole in the seat tube to make the last bit of my installation work.

To be very clear: I do not recommend doing that.

Drilling holes in bicycle frames can compromise their structural integrity, void warranties and generally create problems you don’t want. As a mechanical engineer with a lot of bike experience, I was comfortable making that decision on my own bike because I knew exactly where the frame is least stressed, but it’s definitely not something I’d advise others to copy.

The lesson here isn’t “drill your frame.” It’s to check whether your bike is actually designed for an internally routed dropper post before ordering one. Had I done that first (basically by shining a flashlight down the empty seat tube and realizing there wasn’t a hole to access the bottom bracket), I could have saved myself quite a bit of trouble and just gotten a dropper post with an external cable run.

And finally, here’s one that isn’t really normal bike gear at all, but that I LOVE bringing on my rides.

I spend a lot of time taking photos and videos of bikes, which presents an obvious problem when I’m both the cyclist and the photographer.

The HOVERAir X1 Pro Max has become one of my favorite solutions. It’s a tiny autonomous flying camera that can follow me around without requiring someone else to pilot it. I used the previous version of this drone for a while until this version came out, and then I immediately upgraded.

It folds down small enough that I basically forget that I even have it in my bag. Despite its small size, it still can automatically track and follow me, even at speeds of over 20 mph (32 km/h). That means I can pull it out during a ride, send it up (it takes off from my palm!) and get tracking shots that would normally require another person riding or running alongside me with a camera.

I especially like the Dolly Track mode, which can create some fantastic moving shots while automatically following me from the sides or the front, instead of just the boring old follow-behind-me drone shots you usually see.

Just be aware that its obstacle avoidance isn’t great when flying sideways or backward, meaning I’ve flown it into walls, fences, and street signs plenty of times already. But I can also report back that somehow the little guy is still working fine. I’m not suggesting that’s part of the official durability testing procedure, but it has certainly become part of mine. Now it’s my go-to drone, and I especially like bringing it on my travels for all the same reasons.

After a list this long, I should probably point out that you don’t actually need most of this stuff.

That’s one of the things I love about bikes. You don’t need a pile of expensive gear to have a good time. Most days, give me an e-bike, a helmet and a direction to point the front wheel, and I’m happy.

But after years of riding e-bikes professionally, recreationally, for exercise and simply to get around, these are the products that I’ve found myself continuing to use.

Sure, some of these are expensive pay-to-play things that are a lot of fun but might not be worth it for the casual rider. And some are just $1 pieces of plastic that keep me from smashing my bike computer into the pavement.

But they’ve all found their way into my life after being battle-tested… and passing!

#4361. Our Long-Term Hyundai Palisade Hybrid Is a Bona Fide Road Tripper

Our Palisade Hybrid has embarked on many long adventures in its first 20,000 miles, and it’s easy to see why.

Everyone at Car and Driver loves a road trip, and it’s clear that our editors play favorites when choosing a long-term car for said road trips. Often when traveling, an editor is rolling deep with family, friends, pets, and gear, so one of our more spacious vehicles usually ends up going along for the ride. With a few large cars at our disposal, the team has options, but after 20,000 miles, it’s clear that our long-term Hyundai Palisade Hybrid tends to be the first choice.

Since our last update around the 10,000-mile mark, the Palisade has seen shorter trips to Elk Rapids and Traverse City in Michigan, as well as to Cedar Point in Ohio, but it’s also made it as far as Colorado and West Virginia. Deputy video editor Carlos Lago loaded the Hyundai with his family, their dog, a travel crib, a dog bed, and luggage, and the Palisade Hybrid handled it all without issue. In the logbook, Lago noted that the Palisade was “smooth, decently powerful, and adept at maintaining the higher freeway speeds up north, though the road and tire noise was louder than I’d like at those speeds.”

See all results for new 2026 Hyundai Palisade Hybrid for sale near 75248

Entry and exit haven’t proved as smooth as the Palisade’s ride, though. Lago—and other editors, including yours truly—bemoaned the hands-free door access, which will occasionally lock the doors instead of unlocking them. At that point, we just pull out the key fob, eliminating the point of that tech entirely.

The Palisade Hybrid’s largely white interior is another point of contention for staffers with kids, friends, and pets that ride in the back seat. Those of us with young children in car seats, particularly rear-facing ones, cringe at the footprints and mess we know is coming. Senior features editor Greg Fink hopped in at around 15,000 miles and wondered, “Is it just me, or is this interior looking a little worse for the wear?” With 20,000 miles still to go, we’re hoping that wear stays within reason.

Testing director Dave VanderWerp thought the Palisade Hybrid was a fantastic family SUV with a lot of features not available in other competitive SUVs, but he was still frustrated by parts of the road-trip experience. He found the cargo hold lacking capacity with the third row in use, though his teenagers did manage to occupy that row comfortably. Folding and unfolding the second row proved tricky for VanderWerp’s passengers. A recall on those seats may have added some difficulty there.

Technical editor Austin Irwin had high praise for the Palisade’s interior: “You can just about close your eyes and imagine you’re driving a Genesis.” That being said, he wasn’t blown away by the hybrid powertrain on the highway, where it was flipping between EV and internal-combustion propulsion too often.

Technical assistant Christi VanSyckle drove the Palisade Hybrid out to Colorado with her husband, daughter, and dogs in tow. “Even after a 15-hour driving day,” she wrote, “the comfort and ride were impressive the entire time.” However, her passengers also had issues stowing the second-row captain’s chairs, choosing instead to just squeeze past them to access the third row. VanSyckle called out the Palisade’s steering during her road trip, appreciating its heft when the going got mountainous.

See all results for new 2026 Hyundai Palisade Hybrid for sale near 75248

Since the last update, the Palisade took one trip to the dealer for its routine 16,000-mile service, which included an oil and filter change, a tire rotation, and the usual inspections. The cabin filter also should have been replaced, per the vehicle’s maintenance schedule, but for some reason, the dealer decided not to change that out. As is, the total for that visit came out to $164.

While we can certainly find tidbits that annoy us (we’re very good at that), our long-term Hyundai Palisade Hybrid doesn’t seem like it will be dethroned as the regent of road trips anytime soon. With 20,000 miles left, perhaps we’ll even be able to figure out how the second-row seats work.

Going up north in Michigan often involves running the gamut of wild game crossing your path. With summer finally here, our trips up north have increased, as has our usage of the Hyundai Palisade Hybrid. Most of the fauna has been completely avoidable—with one exception.

Our 2026 Palisade Hybrid is equipped with factory built-in dash cams in the front and rear of the vehicle. They feature continuous-loop recording and parked motion/impact detection. The footage is stored to a MicroSD card. You can access the footage from the infotainment display and are able to look back at about two weeks' worth of clips (important to remember when you have this SUV in your possession).

Our most interesting recent clip came from managing testing editor David Beard, on his way up to Bear Lake, Michigan. A small bear crossed the Palisade Hybrid's path and didn't quite make it across before the right front corner of the SUV tagged it. Thanks to Beard's speedy reaction time, he slowed the SUV enough that it came away without any damage. As for the bear? At the time, we weren't quite sure. Would you check on a potentially very angry bear in the dead of night? A return trip the following day revealed that everyone appeared to make it out the unfortunate situation unscathed.

Beyond its ability to dodge live animals, the Palisade Hybrid has proven to be a great road-trip SUV. Many of our staffers cannot stop raving about the interior of this new Palisade. Vehicle testing director Dave VanderWerp said it's "comfortable, quiet, and seriously upscale." Buyer's Guide director (and current Genesis owner) Rich Ceppos thinks that "this is a full-fledged luxury car now, good enough to wear a Genesis badge. The ride is creamy, the powertrain smooth and quiet, the interior plush, and infotainment straightforward. It's a properly coddling driving experience." Sarah Taylor, online production assistant, agreed that the interior is comfortable and luxurious and further pointed to the Palisade's smooth ride. She also noted: "Slim A-pillars are much appreciated: no huge blind spots." Buyer's Guide managing editor Drew Dorian, who hauled some friends down to Cedar Point in Ohio, praised the seats. He said, "The adjustable side bolsters are a nice touch, and I even found our long-termer's kinetic seat feature useful after four days of riding rollercoasters."

However, there have been a couple small gripes along the way. VanderWerp thought that the Palisade Hybrid "feels substantially larger and less wieldy than the previous model behind the wheel." And despite all the features it has, the Hyundai is missing one key capability: You cannot lock/unlock the rear doors with a touch of the door handle. That's "something every parent of small children would use daily," he said. As a mom of two handling no less than a purse, backpack, water bottle, and certainly a coffee mug at any given time, I fully agree.

At around 8400 miles, it was time for the Palisade Hybrid to head to the dealer for routine service. This visit included an oil change, tire rotation, and multipoint inspection for a total of $146. In addition, there was an open recall that needed to be addressed. Recall 297 pertains to the third-row seatbelt and wiring harness. If the third-row seatbelt is quickly pulled and creates sudden tension, the internal wiring harness could break or become unseated. Luckily, we had not experienced this problem. The dealer inspected the belt buckle and then installed a wiring harness extension to relieve the tension, which was all covered under warranty. Speaking of recalls and seats, our Palisade also got an over-the-air-update fix for the unfortunate issue with the power second- and third-row seats that initially had inadequate pinch detection and caused a brief stop-sale for the new Palisade.

With another 30,000 miles to go, there's no telling where the Palisade Hybrid will take us next. Wherever it goes, we hope the on-board cameras don't pick up any more encounters with bears—or other wildlife.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 11,265 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 25 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 18.2 gal Observed Fuel Range: 450 milesService: $146 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0Damage and Destruction: $0

Hybrids continue popping up in greater numbers across the three-row SUV segment, and one such flower has grown tall enough to catch our eye rather quickly. After Hyundai introduced the redesigned Palisade for 2026, we snagged the new hybrid variant for our annual 10Best competition, where it became an instant favorite. We decided to bring in the new award winner for an in-depth 40,000-mile evaluation.

We ended up with the top-trim Palisade Hybrid Calligraphy model, which starts at a modest $60,380, including the $2000 upcharge for all-wheel drive. Under the hood lies a turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-four and two electric motors nestled within the standard six-speed automatic transmission. Since the Calligraphy is the Palisade's poshest trim, its list of standard equipment is pretty long, including all manner of active safety equipment, rain-sensing wipers, nappa-leather seats with massage for the driver, a tow hitch, a digital rearview mirror, power-adjustable second-row seats, and a head-up display. The only added option on the car was a $245 set of carpeted floor mats, bringing our Palisade Hybrid's total to $60,625.

Our initial testing brought in some respectable numbers for this large hybrid, which produces 329 horsepower and 339 pound-feet of torque. The SUV hustled to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds. Top-gear passing from 50 to 70 mph took place in a tidy 4.4 seconds, and the Palisade sprinted through the quarter-mile in 15.0 seconds at 94 mph. It managed 0.84 g of lateral grip around the skidpad (more than most families will need) and required just 170 feet to stop from 70 mph.

Unfortunately, it didn't take long for our latest long-termer to hit a snag. Upon receiving our new Palisade Hybrid, we began our normal long-term onboarding process, which consists of removing the wheels and measuring the thickness of the brake pads. When we went to remove the pads, we found a wheel stud that was already stripped and spinning in place. The Palisade was promptly whisked away to the dealer and then disappeared for two months. Upon its return, we learned the dealer had to drill out the wheel stud and replace the damaged wheel hub. Ouch.

From there, it took only two weeks before another issue popped up: The engine started overheating. As soon as the car reached higher speeds—especially on the highway—the dashboard would launch into a series of chimes and warnings alerting us that the engine temperature was nearing the danger zone. The Hyundai went back to the dealer, who informed us that the water-pump belt had shredded itself alive. A new belt was installed, attachment points were tightened down, and we were assured it shouldn't happen again.

The dealer also took care of a few recalls and service bulletins that had cropped up. The service department replaced front-bumper wiring related to the active front air flaps and installed two software updates, one of which was required to prevent potential instrument-cluster failure. All repairs and recalls were done under warranty at no cost.

Since the Palisade Hybrid returned for a second time, we've had no further issues. It went on a spring-break road trip to South Carolina and got back with no problems. We are hoping for more of the same as we rack up the miles on this well-dressed family hauler.

#4359. E-quipment highlight: Mantsinen 200 material handler has tank treads

Are you a port or rail terminal operator looking for a new electric material handler that can move serious cargo without sacrificing maneuverability? Do you wish it had tank treads? If that’s you, the Mantsinen 200 might be just the thing.

Designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks. And, yes: I said tracks.

By far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw. And while, yes – most big material handlers have similar form factors, there’s something about the 200 that really sells the whole Dragon Walker vibe.

The Mantsinen 200 is powered by a 380 kW (~510 hp) grid-connected electric motor running at 1,800 rpm. Power comes from a 460V electrical connection as standard, with other voltage options available to suit local site requirements.

Mantsinen says its electrically powered machines deliver the same performance as their diesel counterparts, while eliminating exhaust emissions at the machine and reducing operating noise, energy consumption and maintenance costs. Power is delivered through a load-sensing hydraulic system featuring four variable-displacement piston pumps and a separate closed-loop swing circuit.

Mantsinen also fits the 200 with its proprietary HybriLift energy-recovery system. HybriLift works a lot like regenerative braking by capturing potential energy as the main boom is lowered, but instead of storing that energy as electricity in a battery, the material handler stores it in hydraulic accumulators for reuse during the next lift. The company claims HybriLift improves the big machine’s energy efficiency by up to 50%, effectively giving the machine an additional 300 (ish) hp of lifting assistance at average lifting speed.

And, while the machine normally draws power from the grid, operators aren’t necessarily tethered to an outlet. Mantsinen offers an optional PowerPack that allows the machine to disconnect from its main power supply and still travel around the worksite, with some basic hydraulic systems still functional. The PowerPack is currently diesel-powered, but a battery-backed version isn’t out of the question. It’s a useful bit of flexibility for terminal operators who want the benefits of electric material handling without giving up the ability to reposition the machine when a fixed electrical connection isn’t available.

What do you guys think – is this big material handler the thing you need for your logging or scrapyard, or are you holding out for something even bigger? Let us know in the comments.

#4358. This Little Electric Truck Looks Like France's Answer To The Slate

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Slate made a big splash with its affordable, heavily customizable electric truck. Someone even copied the formula over to a lineup of gas-powered trucks, and we'll see another cheap electric truck from Ford next year. But now the French have their own cheap electric truck concept. It's called the Kilow La Bagnole (which literally translates to "the car"), and it's adorable. I need one.

The La Bagnole is one of the most interesting looking cars I've ever seen, It looks like a French Willy's Jeep but with the fully open wheels of F1 car. It only seats two and two different kinds of body styles, Hard Top (basically a pickup truck) and Closed Hard Top (becomes a van). Both can be had with roof bars so you can put all sorts of gear up there. If you get the Hard Top, the side bed rails are made from either resin-bonded wood fiber or Okoume wood. The former makes it look like it's from IKEA, while the latter looks more premium. However, the Okoume wood requires periodic to keep it weather proof.

Both versions come with an optional removable roof, which is pretty awesome. So you can have either a targa-top pickup or van. The standard La Bagnole lacks doors, and only has big metal side bars, but you can option transparent doors, which are neat.

If you want colors, boy can you get 'em. Kilow offers 12 different regular color options, six gradient colors, and six sparkly "Memories" colors. The best part is that they're all free options. The chassis of the La Bagnole is steel, but all of its body panels are easy removable. So if one breaks or dents, you can just replace it.

There are a few different battery options. Two of the options are made to allow unlicensed drivers to use them. Both the 6 kWh and 12 kWh "Long Range" batteries require no license, as they're classified as quadricycles and capped at 45 km/h (28 mph). Trucks with the 6 kWh battery have only 70 km (43 miles) of range. Cars with the 12 kWh battery can go 164 km (102 miles). The third option mates the 12 kWh battery with an increased speed limiter of 80 km/h (50 mph), but that requires a driver's license.

I love this little thing, and I wish it was coming to the United States. As of right now, it will only be offered in Europe, starting in France. The La Bagnole is such a charming, fun looking little utility vehicle that seems designed equally for function and form. With prices ranging from €10,800 ($11,758) - €13,690 ($14,904), it's an affordable work vehicle for anyone who needs one and stays local, but with tons of character.

#4357. Could a giant catapult launch someone to space? Short answer: Yes.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 8:55 AM EST

For as long as humans have looked at the night sky, we’ve wondered what lies beyond Earth—and dreamed up ways of getting up there. These days, powerful rockets carrying tons of fuel are the tried-and-true method of escaping the planet’s gravitational pull and reaching space.

But what if, instead of modern rockets, we went medieval? Could a trebuchet or catapult—the massive siege weapons once used to fling stones at castles—launch a person into orbit? And if so, just how big would one have to be?

The answer requires a little imagination, a lot of physics, and a space-launching siege weapon of truly ridiculous proportions.

A catapult is essentially a giant lever used to hurl projectiles. Typically, they have a large, spoon-shaped throwing arm that’s wrenched back, creating tension, and then released, flinging an object over a great distance.

A trebuchet is a kind of catapult that uses a counterweight and gravity to launch projectiles. This machine’s long arm rests on a fulcrum, with a sling or cup for the projectile at one end and a heavy counterweight at the other.

When the arm is released, gravity pulls the counterweight downward, sending the opposite end—and its payload—soaring upward and forward.

Trebuchets are typically more powerful than catapults because they can launch heavier payloads over greater distances. So for our purposes, we’ll be focusing on a space trebuchet rather than a space catapult.

Trebuchets have been hurling heavy objects through the air for centuries. The structures are believed to have originated in China as early as the fifth century BC and eventually spread across Eurasia, becoming a formidable force in medieval warfare.

They arrived in Europe during the 12th century and quickly surpassed simple catapults.

Today, trebuchets are no longer used as weapons. But they remain popular as teaching tools for demonstrating physics principles—and for the decidedly more wholesome pursuit of seeing how far we can fling pumpkins, cabbages, and other projectiles.

So let’s crunch the numbers: Could a massive trebuchet really blast a human into orbit? Theoretically, yes. Practically, no.

For help answering this question, Popular Science turned to Frankie Zhu, an assistant professor in space robotics at the Colorado School of Mines in Golden, Colorado. Zhu gamely agreed to do some back-of-the-napkin math to put some numbers to this wildly improbable scenario.

“It just reminds me of a classic physics problem you would encounter in undergrad,” she says.

Before we can get to the heart of the calculations, Zhu says, we need to define some initial parameters. First, because the energy required to send a human into orbit depends on both mass and velocity, we need to know our imaginary astronaut’s mass. Zhu recommends 70 kilograms, or about 154 pounds.

Next, we need to define where space—and, for our purposes, orbit—begins. The conventional boundary is the Kármán line, an imaginary line 100 kilometers (about 62 miles) above sea level that is widely used to mark the edge of space. It’s the point at which Earth’s atmosphere becomes too thin for conventional aircraft to generate enough lift to stay aloft. “An orbit at 100 kilometers would be the lowest energy orbit possible,” she says.

To orbit Earth at the Kármán line—and not plummet back to the ground—a person needs to travel at approximately 7.85 kilometers per second, or 17,500 miles per hour, the same speed the International Space Station travels while orbiting Earth. “Any less and the human would fly up and then come back down in a parabolic trajectory,” she says.

If we assume that the atmosphere doesn’t produce drag on the human as they fly, then the velocity of the person leaving the trebuchet immediately after launch needs to be at least 7.97 kilometers per second, or 17,828 miles per hour. That extra bit of speed accounts for the energy needed to climb from Earth’s surface to the Kármán line.

To launch a human at that velocity, the trebuchet would need to store a massive amount of potential energy—about 2.22 billion joules, by Zhu’s calculations, similar to about 1,200 pounds of TNT. Zhu notes that she’s assuming 100 percent mechanical efficiency, meaning that none of the trebuchet’s stored energy is lost to friction, air resistance, sound, deformation, or the movement of the machine itself.

From here, we can move on to the design of the trebuchet. Based on Zhu’s math, the trebuchet would need a 5,000-ton counterweight—the equivalent of roughly 950 African bush elephants—which would need to drop at least 45.2 meters, or roughly 148 feet.

To turn the relatively slow movement of the massive counterweight into a hypersonic launch speed, the trebuchet would need an extreme mechanical leverage ratio of 379:1, she says. With these figures in mind, the trebuchet’s long throwing arm—the part with the human at the end of it—would need to be about 17.14 kilometers, or 10.7 miles, long.

“That should give you all the physical parameters of the trebuchet, ignoring some physics and human welfare,” she jokes.

How exactly would a human fare under these conditions? Fighter jet pilots can survive up to nine Gs using specialized G-suits, physical straining techniques, and intense centrifuge training. But, Zhu says, the “amount of Gs that the trebuchet is going to reach is…definitely past nine Gs. This human is not going to be alive when they make it to orbit.”

Another hurdle? Building the trebuchet. “To design a structure that can handle that amount of mass—the 5,000-ton counterweight—to support that mass and then to make something that large… that would be a humanity feat and a structural feat,” she says.

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

A more human-friendly option, she says, might be a railgun, which uses electromagnetic forces to accelerate a projectile along a pair of conductive rails at extremely high speeds. To launch a person into orbit, a railgun would also need to be “really, really long,” she says. But because the human projectile could accelerate over a much greater distance and for a longer period of time, a railgun would theoretically offer a smoother acceleration profile—one that’s more amenable to human survival.

“Whereas [with] a trebuchet, the acceleration is going to be impulsive,” she says. “It’s going to be a huge smack at the very beginning if the structure doesn’t flex, if the structure is rigid.”

Rockets have been the standard for launching things into space since 1944, when Germany’s V-2 became the first human-made object to cross the Kármán line. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re the most efficient way to get there.

Rockets require enormous amounts of fuel, and all of that propellant has to be carried onboard. In other words, a rocket has to spend fuel lifting not just its payload, but also the fuel it needs to keep accelerating. This makes getting off Earth an inherently energy-intensive—and expensive—proposition.

With that in mind, engineers continue to explore other ways of getting into space, ideally using less fuel and resources. So far, though, most of their ideas haven’t made it off the drawing board—and, after crunching the numbers, Zhu says it’s highly unlikely that trebuchets will ever replace rockets.

“A lot of ideas are fantastical, some are possible, and an even smaller set are economical,” says Zhu.

#4356. Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

Toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

And when Toyota says compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the company is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

Toyota calls the new Scion a “freedom lab” where the company can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota showed its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

And I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota says the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

Toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

Believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota says his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

Toyota hasn’t announced the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t announced production plans or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota says a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

I’m obviously a big believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

But hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.

#4354. Ford Has A Dedicated Battery Abuse Team. It Obsesses Over How Cells Fail

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Electric vehicle batteries live a harder life than the ones in your phone or laptop. They spend most of their time outdoors, deal with extreme heat and cold, and can take a beating from road debris and potholes.

That means for battery makers, engineering for durability is a priority right up there with energy density and charging speed. And to make sure its cells can handle the abuse of daily life as an EV, Ford has a team dedicated to understanding how batteries fail—and how to stop it.

“That team is 100% focused on battery abuse, design, and testing as a function,” Wesley Thibault, the global chief engineer of battery product development at Ford said last week during a media roundtable at the automaker’s new battery plant in Marshall, Michigan.

Ford is new to the EV battery business. Last week, it started cranking out lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, using technology licensed from China’s CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. The batteries will power the all-important Ford Fathom pickup, which the automaker says will enter production toward the end of next year and kick off a new generation of vastly better and more profitable EVs.

Despite the licensing deal, Ford officials said they were involved in developing the batteries from the outset, with a focus on durability.

The job is not as simple as it sounds. The battery abuse team isn’t tasked with destroying fully made cells and then finding ways to make them indestructible. Instead, Thibault said, it is involved in the design process from the start.

“They want to understand down to the physics level, how a cell fails and why, and when it does fail, how we can prevent it from creating harm to the occupants,” he said.

Quality operator at Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan.

For example, the team measures how cells vent, a crucial process that keeps batteries from catching fire or damaging themselves when they overheat. When temperatures inside a cell get too high, the electrolyte, the liquid chemical that shuttles electrons between the anode and cathode, gets hot and releases gases.

If those gases stay trapped, they can cause short circuits or thermal runaway, so they need to escape in a controlled way. Thibault said his team can measure all of this analytically—using computer models—before the cells are validated.

Production adds another layer of scrutiny. At various stages, the materials inside the cell, as well as the finished cell itself, go through thousands of quality checks, Ford engineers said. Those include CT scans, X-ray machines, lasers, camera inspections, and AI systems.

For example, when the anode slurry is coated onto a copper foil, every millimeter is scanned by lasers for wrinkles and other anomalies. All employees have the ability to pause production if they spot any problems.In case of any issues, they quarantine the cells affected during a specific time period. Ford also claimed that impacted components can be traced all the way from production to the vehicle they end up in.

To be sure, not all of this is unique to Ford. Strict quality checks like these are common among major battery makers, who all aim to minimize scrap rates for costly batteries and maximize the amount of material that actually gets sold.

Ford engineer operating a winding machine, which brings together the anode and cathode, adding a separator in between.

Ford continuously tests the manufacturing process in other ways, too. Engineers said they intentionally feed damaged components and cells—which they call “red rabbits”—into the production machinery to confirm the quality systems catch them and are working as intended.

When cells are almost ready, they’re blasted with helium gas to check for leaks. Once a pack is assembled, it’s mounted on a hydraulic shaker that mimics thousands of miles and years of real-world road use. The shaker can twist, dive, squat, contort, yaw, and replicate the other movements of a car, putting the pack through everything it would see on the road.

Ford’s EV batteries have fared well, by and large. High-mileage Mach-Es with 100,000 or even 200,000 miles on the odometer show little range loss compared to their original capacity, according to data the company released this month.

On the other hand, Ford’s emphasis on battery quality isn’t exactly surprising. The company has grappled with high warranty costs in recent years. And both the Mustang Mach-E and the F-150 Lightning have had issues linked to their high-voltage batteries. Some early Mach-Es were recalled because their battery contactors would overheat during DC fast-charging. A small number of Lightnings were recalled in 2023 due to defective battery cells.

Ford will want to avoid any similar quality issues as it rolls out the high-stakes Fathom, which it hopes will outsell its previous EVs and set the stage for an electric comeback. It will be years before we know how the Fathom's batteries hold up in the real world. For now, it looks like the company is pulling out all the stops to make sure things go off without a hitch.

At $99, the Milwaukee M18 brushless 1/2-inch compact drill/driver kit is the cheapest clean on-ramp into Milwaukee’s M18 battery platform. Measuring 5.7 inches front to back, it fits inside cabinets and between joists without forcing awkward angles. Milwaukee rates the motor at 550 inch-pounds of torque and up to 1,700 rpm, and the box includes one 2.0Ah battery, a charger and a soft bag. If you drive more lag bolts and deck screws than you drill holes, grab the matching M18 compact brushless impact driver kit for the same $99 (or check our picks for the best impact drivers).

Two 4.0Ah batteries, a charger and a free tool

Buy the batteries and the tool comes free. The Ridgid 18V Max Output starter kit pairs two 4.0Ah packs and a charger for $149, and The Home Depot discounts one eligible item in your cart to $0. Standouts on the eight-item menu include a brushless 6-1/2-inch circular saw, a mid-torque impact wrench, an angle grinder, a jigsaw and a 6.0Ah battery. Don’t skip the paperwork after delivery: Ridgid’s Lifetime Service Agreement covers free parts and service on eligible tools bought at The Home Depot, but only if you register them and upload proof of purchase within 90 days.

Hanging a gallery wall or a run of cabinets goes faster with a plumb line already projected across the room. Down to $49.97 from $95, the Bosch GLL50-20 self-leveling cross-line laser casts red horizontal and vertical lines rated out to 50 feet, with an IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating. It runs on included AA batteries (Bosch sells a 3.7V rechargeable pack separately) and mounts via magnets or a 1/4-inch-20 thread (standard camera-tripod mount). Like most red-beam lasers, this model is built strictly for indoor work; step up to a pricier green-beam pick from our guide to the best laser levels if you work in bright, sunlit rooms.

Four other brands mirror the Ridgid starter kit above: add the qualifying battery or combo kit to your cart and select a free tool at checkout. The Ryobi ONE+ starter kit is the lowest buy-in at $99, while the $199 DeWalt 20V Max 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah starter kit unlocks 14 free options (check your ZIP code at checkout, as high-value bare tools sell out unevenly by store). A higher amp-hour (Ah) rating means longer runtime—2.0Ah packs keep drills light overhead, while 4.0Ah to 6.0Ah packs keep circular saws and grinders from bogging down.

Milwaukee’s 12V (M12) and 18V (M18) batteries don’t cross over, and anything labeled “tool only” ships without a battery or charger. Fuel marks Milwaukee’s flagship brushless tier, while Packout refers to its interlocking modular toolbox system. Note that the half-off M18 5-tool combo kit ($349) and 9-tool combo kit ($699) are not Fuel sets and mix in older brushed tools—fine for weekend projects, but check the box list if you want all-brushless gear. The M12 4.0Ah battery two-pack also drops to $79, and the $99 M18 drill kit sits near the top of this page.

Don’t scroll past the 20V Max brushless 3-speed oscillating multi-tool kit at $99—getting the tool, a charger and a 4.0Ah battery at half price is one of the quietest steals in this sale. Meanwhile, watch out for the two standalone drills: the $129 20V Max drill/driver kit throws in two tiny 1.3Ah packs, but its DCD771 uses an older brushed motor. Most shoppers are better off spending $30 less on the $99 Atomic compact drill/driver kit, which trades the spare battery for a shorter brushless tool and a higher-capacity 2.0Ah pack (or stepping up to the $169 Atomic 2-tool kit at the top of the page). For decoding DeWalt’s labels below: Atomic is its compact tier, XR is its pro-grade line and FlexVolt packs power both 20V and 60V tools.

Ryobi delivers the lowest kit prices in this roundup, though the cheapest drill deserves a caveat. The $49.97 ONE+ 3/8-inch drill/driver kit tops out at 600 rpm and lacks an adjustable clutch, making it easy to strip screws or overdrive fasteners. Spend $9 more on the ONE+ 1/2-inch drill/driver kit for a two-speed gearbox and real torque control. HP designates Ryobi’s brushless lineup, and if you already own a charger, the $99 4.0Ah battery two-pack is worth weighing against the $99 starter kit plus free tool listed earlier.

Skip the $149 two-battery starter kit if you only need one tool and a single pack: Ridgid’s $99 shelf includes a 4.0Ah battery with the 1/2-inch impact wrench kit, the 6-1/2-inch circular saw kit and the angle grinder kit.

The headline benchtop cut is $200 off the DeWalt DWS780 12-inch sliding miter saw ($449), which uses an LED shadow-line cut indicator instead of a laser you have to recalibrate and tilts both left and right (double-bevel) so you don’t have to flip long trim boards. Note that the two pneumatic nailers below—the $99 DeWalt brad nailer and the $199 Makita AN924 framing nailer (which takes 21-degree plastic-collated nail strips)—require an air compressor and hose sold separately.

If you’re rounding out a new drill or saw—or grabbing stocking stuffers—consumables start under $10 with the Ryobi 40-piece drill and impact drive kit at $9.97, and the Diablo framing blade two-pack is $12.88.

#4352. Tesla Cybertruck’s already impressive turning radius gets even tighter

Tesla is rolling out an update that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.

But there’s a catch. It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla plans to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.

Tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path. “Even tighter turns now rolling out to new Cybertrucks,” the account wrote.

In a follow-up post, Tesla said the improvement requires software version 2026.44 or newer and “only applies to model year 2027 Cybertrucks.”

It's not the size … it's how you maneuver itEven tighter turns now rolling out to new Cybertrucks pic.twitter.com/FuNoox4ax0

Tesla didn’t share a new turning circle figure. In the video, the “after” circle is visibly smaller than the “before” one by what looks to be at least a foot.

The Cybertruck’s maneuverability comes from its rear-wheel steering paired with steer-by-wire. At low speeds, the rear wheels turn opposite to the fronts, which shrinks the space the truck needs to make a U-turn. We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s four-wheel steering since the prototype days, when Tesla was showing it off in parking garages.

Even before this update, the results were impressive. Tesla’s owner’s manual lists the Cybertruck’s curb-to-curb turning circle at about 43.5 ft (13.25 m). That beats the Ford F-150 Lightning at roughly 47.8 ft and the Rivian R1T at 44.9 ft, and it’s within about 4 ft of a Model Y. Not bad for a 6,600-lb truck that’s nearly 19 feet long.

And Tesla always said there was more to come. At launch, the rear wheels turned only about 3 degrees. In early 2024, a Tesla engineer said a software update would push that to 10 degrees, and Elon Musk said the company had improvements in the works to “tighten the turning circle significantly.”

Tesla hasn’t said whether this update delivers the full 10 degrees, or why it’s limited to 2027 trucks. If it comes down to hardware, owners of earlier Cybertrucks who were counting on this as an over-the-air upgrade are out of luck.

Credit where it’s due. The turning circle is one of the best things about the Cybertruck, and anyone who has driven one knows it. Steer-by-wire combined with rear-wheel steering is real engineering, and other vehicles are just starting to get that combo a couple years after Cybertruck had it. Making it even better is a nice update.

And 39.4 feet turning circle for the Cadillac Escalade which also has rear wheel steering. As does the iX5 (39.7'), MB GLC (36.7') and EQS (35.8'), the Lucid Gravity (38.4), Hummer 37.4', Cayenne (38.4) and a around two dozen other vehicles on the market today. So maybe this is not such big news after all?

Earlier this month, Musk announced that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab. He has since pushed the end date to the end of summer 2027 to work through an “order backlog.” We estimate Tesla is delivering about 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks a quarter, roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year it planned for.

So Tesla is improving a 2027 model year truck that it will stop making next summer. And since Tesla now only sells the $109,990 Cyberbeast, the people getting this upgrade are the few still buying the most expensive Cybertruck in its final months. It does nothing about what actually sank the truck: pricing that never came close to the $39,900 promised in 2019, range and towing that fell short, and a design most truck buyers never warmed up to.

It’s a cool engineering flex on a product with an expiration date. If Tesla had delivered this kind of polish on the $40,000 truck it promised, would we be writing the Cybertruck’s obituary right now?

#4351. VW’s Cheap EVs Are So Popular, Buyers Face Wait Times Of Nearly Two Years

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen, along with its group siblings, Skoda and Seat, are facing huge demand for their small electric cars, which in turn is leading to wait times that are nearing two years in some cases.

With over 50,000 orders on tap already, the Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchback is one of the most successful models from the Volkswagen Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family, with the most affordable trim having wait times of up to 21 months in Germany, according to Spanish outlet Motor.es. That’s double compared to the 10-month wait times reported earlier this year.

Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo production in Martorell, Spain

It’s a similar story when it comes to the technically similar Skoda Epiq, with over 80,000 orders since its introduction and wait times of up to 17 months for the most popular versions. The Cupra Raval, meanwhile, has amassed roughly 50,000 orders and has faced a multi-day production halt at the Martorell plant in Spain, where it shares an assembly line with the ID. Polo.

Together, the four models that make up the group’s affordable EV family, namely the Volkswagen ID. Polo, the Cupra Raval, the Skoda Epiq, and the Volkswagen ID. Cross, have attracted approximately 150,000 orders in Europe since their debut through the end of September.

It’s worth noting that while the cheap trims of all these cars, which start at around €24,995 ($27,300) in Germany, have put the Volkswagen Group in an unfavorable position, the more expensive versions are scheduled to ship a lot faster. The ID. Polo Sportline currently has a five-month wait time, while customers of the ID. Polo GTI have to wait roughly seven months.

The higher-than-expected demand has put all automakers at the mercy of battery cell suppliers. Currently, the Martorell factory that assembles the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval is working double shifts and has a daily output of up to 1,000 vehicles, but work has already begun to add a third shift, which would increase output to 1,200 vehicles daily.

The expansion is tied to battery production, and while there’s a factory nearby that can build up to 1,200 packs per day, it relies on cells that come from an external supplier. The same goes for the Pamplona plant that assembles the Volkswagen ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq electric crossovers. The two EVs share the same assembly line as VW’s combustion-powered T-Cross and Taigo, both of which bring in more money than their battery-powered counterparts.

A Volkswagen spokesperson told Germany's Automobilwoche that demand has increased “significantly more dynamically than originally expected” and that ramping up production “cannot be adjusted short-term to the same extent as this dynamically increasing demand.”

More employees are being added to the workforce, and Gotion’s new cell factory in Spain is expected to be fully operational early next year, which should help the automaker boost production without relying on outside help.
